subject: Private fleet admission gate & network fence — VectorCloud capacity request
messages:
From: Rajiv Menon <rajiv.menon@vectorcloud.com>
To: aditya_rao@redwood.ai
Cc: VectorCloud Ops <ops@vectorcloud.com>
Date: 2027-06-19T09:12:00-07:00
Subject: Private deployment sizing request — VectorCloud

Hi Aditya,

Thanks for taking this. We are kicking off a private deployment (VPC) with Redwood for a new VectorCloud service tier that will be on-prem in our east-coast datacenter. We need help turning our high-level QPS/latency targets into a concrete admission policy + network/fleet sizing plan. High level: 

- Expected steady-state load: 1,200 toks/s (model: Llama-87B q4_0) across 250 concurrent low-latency sessions.
- Peak pattern: 10x short spikes (10s) ~ every 3 hours, sustained over a day for launches.
- Latency targets: p95 < 120ms, p99 < 350ms for chat completions (50–200 tokens).
- Egress constraints: limited cross-rack backplane (10 Gbps per rack), and strict egress billing we want to keep below 18 TB/day.

We need a mutual action plan that covers: admission controls (how we gate bursts), headroom targets for GPUs/NICs, cache warmup and KV cache priming strategy, fallback routing (hosted -> dedicated -> degraded model) and the exact network configuration required (NICs, MTU, allowed ports, SNAT sizing).

Can you provide: 1) a recommended node/GPU count and reserve headroom; 2) admission controller param ranges (token-bucket rates, max queue depth); 3) network egress and cross-AZ guardrails; and 4) a short ops checklist we can run during cutover.

If possible, include any short simulation traces or a quick-run script we can execute on our side. I'll pull in our infra lead after your initial proposal.

Best,
Rajiv
Director of Platform Engineering
VectorCloud

From: aditya_rao@redwood.ai
To: Rajiv Menon <rajiv.menon@vectorcloud.com>
Cc: laura_bennett@redwood.ai, grace_oconnor@redwood.ai
Date: 2027-06-19T13:45:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Private deployment sizing request — VectorCloud

Rajiv — thanks, this is clear and actionable. Attached are three artifacts: a network checklist, a mutual-action-plan draft, and a small set of simulation traces that mirror the burst pattern you described. High-level answers below; I followed up with our infra team for precise simulation runs and we'll include those traces.

1) Sizing & headroom (initial recommendation):
- Baseline pool: 8 nodes, 4x A100 equivalent GPUs per node (32 GPUs total) to meet sustained 1,200 toks/s with batching tuned to 1–2 requests per batch for latency-sensitive sessions.
- Burst absorption: reserve 15% GPU headroom (additional 5 GPUs spare) and maintain a warm pool of 2 nodes pre-primed for KV cache to reduce cold-start P99.
- NICs: 100 Gbps uplink per node recommended; if constrained to 25/40 Gbps, increase node count by ~25% to avoid egress saturation.

2) Admission controller parameters (starting ranges):
- Token bucket rate: set steady_rate = 1,400 toks/s (10–15% above expected steady) with burst_capacity = 12,000 tokens (allows ~10s spike at 10x before shedding).
- Queue depth: limit request queue to 120 concurrent inflight per node (beyond this, early reject with 429 & retry-after).
- Backpressure strategy: priority for pinned/SLAs routes, then best-effort. Use adaptive token refill based on observed p95 latency window (30s).

3) Network & egress guardrails:
- Cross-rack backplane: ensure per-rack egress limiters (software policers) that cap to 70% of physical link to avoid microbursts; set policer at 7 Gbps for your 10 Gbps links.
- MTU: enable jumbo frames (9000) across the inference path to reduce CPU overhead for large KV transfers.
- SNAT pool size: allocate 512 SNAT ports per host for concurrent upstream calls (monitor TO).
- TLS: mutual TLS to our control plane; customer-managed KMS for model keys.

4) Ops checklist (cutover):
- Pre-warm: spin warm pool 48h before cutover with representative prompts; confirm KV hit rate > 60%.
- Canary: route 1% traffic for 24h, validate p95/p99 and token-bucket behaviour.
- Failover: set automated fallback to a 13B quantized variant (hosted) when admission rejects exceed 2% for 15m.
- Observability: enable token-level tracing for the first 72h and export p99 histograms to the shared Drive folder.

Attachments: privgpu-network-checklist.pdf, mutual-action-plan-draft.docx, simulation-traces-6-19.tar.gz

I'll coordinate a short architecture review next week and include our simulation outputs. If you want different headroom (more conservative), I can show a 20% headroom variant.

Best,
Aditya Rao
Sr. Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference

From: vivek_kulkarni@redwood.ai

Date: 2027-06-21T11:20:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Private deployment sizing request — VectorCloud (sim notes)

Laura / Aditya — ran a quick sim covering the token-bucket ranges and cache hit variation you asked for. Key findings and suggested parameters below (raw traces attached to the MAP):

- Admission controller tuning: steady_rate = 1,400 toks/s, burst_capacity = 12k tokens gives p95 ~ 95ms and p99 ~ 310ms at 60% cache hit. If cache hit drops to 30% p99 jumps to ~520ms.
- Recommendation: couple admission with an early-shed policy at 110% sustained (return 429 + short retry window) rather than letting queues grow. This avoids tail amplification from queueing.
- GPU headroom: 15% reserve is the sweet spot for your burst profile; 20% gives a smaller p99 tail but increases cost materially.
- Batch sizing: 1–2 dynamic batch window for chat; larger batches (4–8) only for non-interactive bulk endpoints.
- CPU/NIC overhead: we observed ~8–10% CPU spike during bursts for KV marshalling; ensure the host has 2 extra cores reserved per GPU for marshalling and networking threads.
- Autoscale cooldown: 120s up, 300s down with warm-pool prefetching to ensure priming completes.

I'll export a pair of PNGs (p99_vs_burst.png, p99_vs_kvhit.png) and add them to the Drive map.

—Vivek
Senior Reliability Engineer
Redwood Inference
